steps.action:
# The Counting

Elias Marsh had kept count of everything for thirty-one years.

He knew it was thirty-one because he had made a mark on the door-frame of the lamp room each January — not a resolution, just a record. He was not a man who believed in resolutions. He believed in records. In the lamp room, he kept a logbook that listed every ship he had seen, every storm he had weathered, the wind speed and direction at six a.m. and six p.m. every day, the temperature of the water as measured by a gauge on the south-facing dock, and the number of times the fog horn had sounded each month.

He knew the lighthouse had stood on Cray's Point since 1887. He knew the original lens had been a third-order Fresnel, and that the current lens — installed in 1954, replaced again in 1991 — rotated once every four seconds and could be seen from eighteen nautical miles on a clear night. He knew these things because knowing them felt like holding the lighthouse in his hands, which was the closest thing to comfort he had found since Margaret died.

Margaret had died in March, eleven years ago. He had written that in the logbook, too: *March 14. Wind: SW, 12 knots. Temp: 41°F. Fog: intermittent. Margaret gone.*

He had not been able to write more than that.

---

It was a Wednesday in October when the boy appeared.

The storm had been building since noon, and by eight in the evening the wind had reached forty knots and the sea was the color of pewter hammered by an anxious hand. Elias was in the lamp room checking the rotation mechanism — it had developed a slight drag in wet weather, a problem he had reported twice to the Coast Guard without resolution — when he saw the light.

Not his light. A small light, low on the water, half a mile to the southwest. It moved erratically, disappearing behind swells and then reappearing, tilted at angles that made Elias's stomach clench. He was already moving.

He had done this before — not often, but enough. He knew the path down the rocky slope in the dark the way he knew the sound of his own breathing. He kept a skiff tied at the dock, a flat-bottomed aluminum thing that he hated but trusted, and he put it in the water without thinking, because the thinking had already been done long ago, on the first night he had seen a light like that one and understood what it meant.

The water was terrible. He would write that in the log later: *Seas: 8-10 ft, confused. Conditions: terrible.* He rowed because the outboard would not start in this — it never started in this — and he rowed toward the tilting light, which was closer now, and then very suddenly close indeed, and the thing he had thought was a sailboat resolved itself into a small wooden dinghy with a sail that had torn loose and was trailing in the water like a broken wing.

In the boat was a boy.

He looked to be about twelve. He was wearing a life jacket that was too large for him, and he was bailing with a plastic bucket, and when Elias came alongside and grabbed the gunwale of the dinghy, the boy looked up with an expression that was not panic but something more exhausting than panic — the look of someone who had been frightened for a very long time and had run out of the energy to show it.

"All right," Elias said, which was not a question.

"I lost the oars," the boy said. "I had oars."

"I see that."

"My dad's going to be upset about the sail."

Elias looked at the ruined sail. "He'll be glad you're alive," he said, and hoped it was true.

He got the boy into the skiff, and the boy sat in the bow and did not say another word while Elias rowed them back through the terrible dark water to the dock. The boy helped tie up — he knew how to tie a cleat hitch, which meant someone had taught him something, which meant someone had tried — and then they went up the path to the lighthouse, and Elias put the boy in the kitchen with a blanket and a cup of tea and called the Coast Guard and then the harbormaster, who said the boy's name was Owen, that his father was already at the station, that they would come in the morning when the weather cleared.

"In the morning?" Elias said.

"Road's flooded at the causeway," the harbormaster said. "Nobody's coming out tonight."

Elias looked at Owen, who was holding the mug with both hands and staring at the table.

"All right," Elias said.

---

He made soup from a can because it was what he had. The boy ate without complaint, which Elias respected. Afterward, he showed Owen the lamp room, because it seemed like the right thing, and the boy stood before the great rotating lens and watched the light sweep the dark water, and his face did something complicated.

"Does it ever show you things?" Owen asked. "Things you don't expect?"

Elias thought about this. "Sometimes. Whales, occasionally. Once, a raft of sea otters holding hands."

Owen looked at him. "They do that?"

"So they don't drift apart in their sleep."

The boy was quiet for a moment. Then he said, "Do you get lonely out here?"

Elias had been asked this before — by the quarterly inspector, by Margaret's sister, by a reporter who had come out years ago looking for something picturesque. He had always said no. He had always meant it as a kind of proof of himself.

But Owen was twelve years old and had been alone in a broken boat in a storm, bailing with a plastic bucket, and had not cried, and was now asking a serious question with serious eyes. He deserved a serious answer.

"Yes," Elias said. "I do."

Owen nodded, as if this confirmed something he had suspected. "But you stay."

"I stay."

"Why?"

Elias looked at the light sweeping the dark. He thought about the ships he had counted, the thirty-one marks on the door-frame, the entry that said *Margaret gone* because he hadn't been able to write more. He thought about the otters holding hands.

"Because the ships need to know where the rocks are," he said. "And there has to be someone who knows."

Owen seemed to consider this. Outside, the storm shook the windows, and the light went on turning, and Elias found that the room felt, just slightly, less empty than it usually did.

"I'll stay up with you," Owen said. "If you want. So you don't have to be alone tonight."

Something in Elias's chest — dense and dark and very heavy for eleven years — shifted. Not gone, not healed, just shifted, the way a stone moves in a current without disappearing.

"I'd like that," he said.

Later, he wrote it in the log between the wind speed and the temperature, in his careful, practiced hand: *October 22. Seas: 8-10 ft, confused. Rescued one (1) boy. Name
